utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll continue to hear the evidence of Mr. Kelecevic through videolink. Could you please confirm, Mr. Registrar at the other side of the videolink, whether you can hear me, whether you can see us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, good morning, Your Honours. We can hear and see you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see and hear you as well. Mr. Kelecevic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony - that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to follow up briefly on a couple of matters we discussed yesterday. First, regarding the Kosmos facility. You testified yesterday at transcript page 37171 that it was under the Main Staff after the transformation. That refers to the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might be in a dilemma. It may have been the Yugoslav General Staff that had certain influence over the corps, because it used to be a maintenance institute for rocket technology and weaponry for the entire JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So do I understand your answer to be that you don't recall which Main Staff had control of it after the transformation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain. It is part of the economic sector that I never became involved in. I never visited any of the maintenance institutes because I did not have sufficient time. As far as I know, from peacetime, the directing authority of the facility was the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, you described at transcript page 37146 how in May and June 1992 General Talic would hold approximately weekly meetings in person with his assistant commanders. You would also attend those meetings yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. Sometimes if the situation on hand was an extraordinary one, I wasn't able to come. I can also say that basically every Monday there was a meeting and information was dispatched in terms of when it would occur. In any case, it was customary to hold it once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that group would discuss events throughout the 1st Krajina Corps' area of responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At any given time, the corps would have a duty team; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps always had an operations team that was on duty around-the-clock. It was always headed by an officer who received all reports from the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that team would report to General Talic [Realtime transcript read in error: "Tolimir"] or, in his absence, to you on the basis of those reports; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I can say this: In 99 per cent of the cases, the commander was always in the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I've been recorded at transcript page 3, line 12, to refer to "General Tolimir." I'd certainly intended to refer to General Talic, and I think from his answer that's how the witness understood the question as well.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And regarding the daily combat reports that the corps would send to the Main Staff, General Talic, or you if he was absent, would always read the daily combat report and be able to speak with the Main Staff about the matters that were discussed in it; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. However, after the 28th of April when I left the command post, which is something I explained yesterday, to a separate axis along the corridor with the group I was with, I did not receive those reports from the basic command post regularly from Gradiska. It was more seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But General Talic would; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talic always received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if he was absent and you were standing in for him, the important matters that you'd have to be available to speak with the Main Staff about would be communicated to you in another way; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could always rely on our communication means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to turn now to Operation Corridor where we left off yesterday. The corridor was opened by the end of June 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But the opening up of the corridor was on the 25th of June, I think, and on that occasion a very narrow channel was opened up. I would even dare say it was just a path, a footpath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Odzak operation that we discussed yesterday, the purpose of that operation was to widen the corridor -- or the purposes of that operation included, among other things, widening the corridor and securing a northern border for Republika Srpska on the Sava River; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is partially correct, because from the main road between Modrica and Derventa and on to Banja Luka, Odzak is perhaps 4 or 5 kilometres away. That area was widened later on. At this point in time, it was still a footpath. Even when one went through the fields, it was the first column that carried medication and oxygen barely got through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I hadn't at this point asked you to describe the path. What I'd asked was the purposes of the Odzak operation included, first, widening the corridor; and, second, achieving a northern border for Republika Srpska on the Sava River. Both of those were among the purposes of liberating Odzak as the VRS described it; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you will, the immediate goal was to secure the general area of Modrica rather than Odzak, as you assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You described yesterday there was ten days of combat around Odzak. We saw evidence that it was shelled, that thousands of people left, so certainly one of the goals was to secure that area and the border on the Sava River; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The goal was to reach the Sava as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the VRS continued to engage in operations to widen the corridor and secure all of the territory bordering on the Sava River during the late summer and early fall of 1992 including, for instance, taking Brod in October of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, the part near Orasje, Domaljevac, and Tolisa near the Sava River, that is something that was never achieved by the VRS. It never reached the banks of the Sava in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the corridor operation in June and July, one of the units that participated in that operation was Veljko Milankovic's unit; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit had not been assigned a separate axis or a zone. At the time, it was not an establishment unit of the 1st Corps. I would say it was a small detachment that for a while was treated as a paramilitary formation, and for a certain period of time we were trying to include it in our ranks but we were never successful. We never militarised it, so to speak, in the full sense of the word so as to be able to consider it a true establishment unit of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have three follow-up questions. First, Milankovic was, in early June 1992, appointed a battalion commander in the 327th Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an attempt of ours. It was a very small unit. We wanted to include it among our scout ranks of the 327th. For a while, it actually worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, you know he was a criminal; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know. I would say he was a petty criminal. He wasn't a criminal that would operate at the national level. He operated locally, I'd say, in Prnjavor municipality and perhaps a little further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he also engaged in looting during his participation in the corridor operation, right, among other crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was engaged in looting. But along the axis where he was operational, he did take some personal advantage and stole some items for himself and the members of his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask now that Mr. Van hooydonk play a video-clip marked as 65 ter 32814b. CLSS has confirmed the transcripts so we'll only need to play it once.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Reporter: ... Serbian people was grieving. In Prnjavor, Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, commander of the Wolves from Mount Vucjak, was buried, who three days ago in the military medical -- who three days ago in the military medical hospital in Belgrade succumbed to the wounds he received on the 4th of February in the village of Hasici in the Republic of Serbian Krajina: "Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, commander of the battalion 'Vukovi sa Vucjaka,' was buried today with all military honours in his native village of Kremna on Mount Vucjak near Prnjavor. Over 20.000 people, young and old, well known and not so well known, came to pay their respects to their legendary commander. Commander Veljko, who immediately at the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia, led his Wolves to liberate the Serbian lands. "Martic: Unfortunately we part with the most courageous, the most resolute heros and sons of our people. Today with a gun salvo at the Dalmatian and other battle-fields in the Serbian Republic, we will announce a forceful enemy offensive for the liberation of the Serbian lands. Respected citizens of Prnjavor, brothers and sisters, Serbian heros, invincible heros from Mount Vucjak in the name of all the heros of the Serbian army and Krajina, accept my deepest condolences. This parting is hard for all of us. Let Veljko's descendants be proud of their father, a hero for Vucjak. Let his mother be proud of her son. Let the Wolves from Mount Vucjak be proud of their courageous brave hero commander. We are convinced that the heros will revenge their commander in the defence of the holy Serbian land and the Serbian people. Although such scenes are present in everyday life, when we part from the best sons of the Serbian people, Veljko, I would like to make an oath on your grave that we will endure till the end. We will have enough strength, prudence, and wisdom to finish what we started. We will do everything so that all Serbs live in one state. "Kelecevic: We always had confidence in you and your Wolves. It was so in western Slavonia. It was so during the breakthrough of the corridor when you brilliantly fulfilled all the tasks. All you had to say about our struggle, you said through action with a gun, with your own example. Since that is the only way to defend these people, to help the Serbs wherever they may be. "Reporter: Although Veljko is no longer with us, while there are Serbs and Serbian people, the song will be sung. Veljko's going, followed by the lads, Serbian volunteers of Mount Vucjak."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the first speaker that we saw praising Milankovic with the moustache, that was Milan Martic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: His forces participated in the corridor operation under the command of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a detachment numbering between 200 and 250 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Under the command of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the command of the VRS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the second --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the second speaker that we saw praising Milankovic was yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 32814b.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video receives number P7471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7471 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn back to May 1992 now, sir. The 1st Krajina Corps carried out what were referred to as disarmament operations in many of the municipalities of its area of responsibility in late May 1992, very shortly after the transformation; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when we say "disarmament," the people purportedly being disarmed, some actually disarmed, some purportedly, were Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't aimed only against the Muslims and Croats. It was aimed against all those who were not authorised to carry personal weapons and who did not hand them over when asked to do so by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to test your evidence about that in a number of different ways. But first, the 1st Krajina Corps took a number of prisoners, a large number of prisoners, during these operations; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And those prisoners who were detained in various camps in the 1st Krajina Corps' area of responsibility, those were entirely or almost entirely Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in late May 1992, General Talic formed an exchange commission to facilitate exchanging prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commission was established, although I don't know when precisely, that was tasked with exchanges. It involved both the VRS as a whole as well as the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32732.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an order by General Talic dated the 29th of May, 1992 ordering that a commission for the exchange of prisoners shall be formed, setting out four members, including President Captain First Class Milutin Grujicic, and setting out which office it will be in, the office of the press centre of the Banja Luka Corps. So a commission at the corps level was formed on or about the 29th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, that was the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32732 receives number P7472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard evidence from Goran Krcmar who served as a member of that exchange commission in 1993 and onwards. He testified as a Defence witness and testified, among other things, that the 1st Krajina Corps had a computerised database of the people it was holding prisoner. Do you recall when that database was created?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. It was a very modest database. Back then, the electronics and computer technology had not advanced that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was used, however, for instance, to provide information to the Main Staff about prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty whether the automatic data processing was used in that regard. In any case, it -- the data provided by the commission was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the commission, the exchange commission, would send its proposals for exchange to the Main Staff for approval; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, the commission sent it to the corps command, and the corps command sent it onwards. I think it followed the line of the assistant commander for morale up the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32104.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see here a document coming from then Colonel Tolimir to the 1st Krajina Corps exchange commission, dated the 21st of January, 1993, and he says: "Your proposal for the exchange of prisoners dated 12 January 1993 has been considered and we give our consent for you to do as you suggested." And this is a reflection of the Main Staff's authority over the exchanges conducted by the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate. As I said, the 1st Corps sent it to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff approved or did not approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 32104 receives number P7473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, many of the prisoners at the 1st Krajina Corps held in 1992 were not members of enemy military forces, they were civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps just had, how do I put this, I mean, that's what the control of the 1st Krajina Corps was, Manjaca and Stara Gradiska. I cannot speak about other camps now, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also please answer the question, whether many of the prisoners were not members of enemy military forces but rather civilians. Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give an answer to that question, whether somebody was a member of the enemy force. In order for somebody to be an enemy, a lot of investigation is necessary so that I could say that somebody is an enemy. There were a lot of Muslims and Croats in our units, too. I cannot say that all of them were enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say investigation was necessary to determine if somebody was an enemy because the circumstances in which these people were taken prisoner didn't indicate they were enemies. They were taken prisoner in their homes, on their fields, non-selectively; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert now how it was that they were taken prisoner, whether it was in a field or whether it was at some barricade or somewhere. I cannot assert anything now. And I could never, I mean, confirm that kind of thing, that they had been taken prisoner in a field or somewhere, in a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, the guards at the Manjaca detention camp told the 1st Krajina Corps' security and intelligence organ that that was how people were being picked up, non-selectively, in their homes, on their fields, people who couldn't be treated as prisoners of war. Colonel Bogojevic knew that and he would have had an obligation to tell you and General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Bogojevic, I've -- that's come up a few times. If I say -- if I mean "Blagojevic," I'll say it very slowly, but otherwise the court reporter can assume that I'm talking about Colonel Bogojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also pronounce it also very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the question. It is Bogojevic, Colonel Bogojevic. I already told you that yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what was that? You wished to say something, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I invited you not to confirm the correction, but I wanted to invite you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started answering that question in relation to what it was that the guards from these camps said. These guards, I can just speak about the Manjaca camp and Stara Gradiska. I cannot say what the procedure was in these other camps, especially Prijedor, Omarska, Kozarac, Keraterm, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would tell us what you do know about the camps you say you have knowledge about and then answer in that way the question put to you by Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about camp Manjaca. The commander ordered that it should be a camp for POWs, and that camp was regulated on the basis of all of those regulations. At least in my view I could say, as far as I know, that there was a full record of who went in, who went out. I believe that there will be other questions about life in the camp, so I will provide answers if that is what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I am just speaking about the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. First I'd like an answer to the question that I asked. The people who were detained there were picked up in their homes, on their fields, unselectively, as both Colonel Bogojevic and you yourself knew; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that anybody had been picked up in the field. I just knew from the reports that there was such and such a number of prisoners and they were in the area of the Manjaca facility. I did not go into that, how people were picked up or how prisoners were brought to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were meeting with Colonel Bogojevic regularly during this period. He knew - and the reference for the parties is P220 - from the guards that people were being picked up that way. It was his obligation to tell you and to tell General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know. I never received that kind of information, that somebody was captured in a field and brought to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There were thousands of prisoners at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the month of August 1992 when the supreme commander issued an order, Radovan Karadzic issued an order, to the effect that -- I mean, from the broader area of Prijedor they should be transferred to Manjaca. Then, in Manjaca, as for work and life of these prisoners, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the 1st Krajina Corps that was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You have not answered a very simple question. There were thousands of prisoners in Manjaca. And just to clarify, that's beginning earlier than August when people from Kljuc and Sanski Most had been picked up and brought in. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that an excellent corps chief of staff has no idea who the people -- who the thousands of people being held prisoner by his corps are?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I had no idea. I know that there was a camp there, I know that they were being treated fairly. I didn't go into anything further because there were the organs for morale, et cetera. There was a commission. There were people who took care of their safety, security, life, and work. I, as chief of staff, did not have the time to deal with that subject matter, how they were brought there and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P2886.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, sir, you said a moment ago that the commander ordered that Manjaca should be a camp. Which commander did you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He gave a name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commander, I meant the corps commander Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But at paragraph 15, I don't know whether this is the answer you're referring to, line 1, the witness said: "From the month of August 1992 when the supreme commander issued an order, Radovan Karadzic issued an order, to the effect that ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just so we have the chronology right and to address Judge Moloto's question as well, it's right that General Talic ordered the camp set up at the beginning of June. Prisoners were brought in from municipalities other than Prijedor in June and July, and then in August, pursuant to the Karadzic order that you've described, the prisoners from Prijedor camps, many of the prisoners from Prijedor camps were transferred to Manjaca as well; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, exactly. But until the month of August, I personally did not pay any visits to that camp. I cannot remember exactly now, but maybe it was August or September, I cannot say now, I did visit a facility and I can speak to you about that, if you're interested. As for the period before August, I did not have any knowledge about life and work in that part of Manjaca, in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll have a few questions about that. But first, what we're looking at on our screens right now, this is the 1st Krajina Corps' analysis of activity concerning elements of combat readiness in 1992. This is a report to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is the main overview of the 1st Krajina Corps's work in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have the bottom of page 12 in English and page 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now returning to the topic of the exchange commission, the 1st Krajina Corps is telling the Main Staff: "We achieved significant results in activities related to prisoner-of-war exchanges. Within the 1st Krajina Corps' zone, over 9.200 prisoners were exchanged of which 2.300 were military personnel from the former BH plus the bodies of around 250 individuals who were killed." Now, this means, first, that 6.900 prisoners were exchanged by the 1st Krajina Corps commission that were not military personnel from the former BH; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these figures. After all, it's been a very long time. And my health hasn't been that good, so I really cannot recall any of these figures. But I believe that since this is contained in the report, I stand by the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You must have reviewed the report at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have. But I don't remember the report because there are five elements of combat readiness there, and now you are just asking me about this particular piece of information and that there is combat readiness, training, policy involved, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand there are other elements of combat readiness. I am asking you about this one. And to be perfectly fair, what I'm putting to you is, setting the specific numbers aside, you can't possibly have forgotten that, according to this report, 75 per cent of the people who had been exchanged were not military personnel. You can't possibly have forgotten that, can you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. I don't know whether it's 70 per cent or whether it's some other figure, but I do know that there were those who were not military-age or military conscripts -- no, not military conscripts. Of military age, able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You knew there were civilians who were detained, first collected in their homes and on their fields, then detained by the 1st Krajina Corps, then exchanged by the 1st Krajina Corps exchange commission; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'll telling you I have no way of knowing whether it was a civilian or a military conscript until certain checks were completed. And on the basis of these checks and if that information was provided to the command, then I could have found out. But I had no way of knowing before that, and now I cannot state whether these were civilians or whether there were some people who were military conscripts as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were trained in the laws of war; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As a JNA officer, you were trained in the laws of war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. At school I studied international law and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What do the laws of war say about detaining thousands and thousands of people and 23 years later having no way of knowing whether there was any basis to detain them?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I cannot tell you how it was that they were taken prisoner. I do not know how they were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You've been quite clear about that, sir. What I'm putting to you is the corps was knowingly and unlawfully detaining thousands of people that it had no basis to detain; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that certain units were not doing that, too, but I personally am not aware of anything being done in that way. Because I had 48 units. Do you understand that? The equivalent of a brigade, regiment, and independent battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it would have been your responsibility and General Talic's if those units were committing crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were doing that - that is to say, if there were civilians there who were not putting up any resistance and who were not disobeying the civilian and military authorities - then, of course, that is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what we see here, 6900 people exchanged that weren't enemy military personnel, that's exactly the sort of people you described, people who weren't putting up any resistance, people who were civilians, people who there was no basis to detain; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I cannot say how long they were detained, but this is also a measure taken by a unit; that is to say, if they said that they were detained unlawfully, then they would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P230.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, you knew, in fact, before August that there were reports from the Red Cross and elsewhere that people were being abused in Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot put it that way. This was a small number. I mean, they were in the Manjaca camp and it was only in August that there was a larger number that merited particular attention; that is to say, having a triage screening carried out, et cetera. I, as chief of staff, did not go into that and did not know of any abuse against these people in this camp. However, if that did happen, I personally believe that these were individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a report by the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 16th of July to the Main Staff and the Doboj operative group labelled for General Talic. It's a report on a visit by the Red Cross to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we see the end of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, what makes you believe that these were individual cases if you at the same time tell us that you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying that I don't know anything. I am saying that I don't know of such cases, that this was abuse en masse, because I believe that the corps command would have taken appropriate measures to stop that, prevent that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we looked at a document a minute ago that more than 6.000 persons not being members of the opposite forces apparently were exchanged as if they were prisoners of war. Wouldn't you have expected that measures would have been taken in respect of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear this question very well, and I did not quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said if it would have been massive abuse, it couldn't have been because otherwise measures would have been taken. That's what I heard you say explaining why you considered those cases of abuse individual cases. Now I ask you that if you've seen a minute ago a report saying that 6.000 persons not being members of the armed forces of the opponent were exchanged as if they were prisoners of war rather than just be released and sent home, would you not have expected then where this was a massive exercise that measures would have been taken there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that 6.000 is a massive figure, but then for as long as that number was there, we did not know that most of them were civilians. Once it was established that they are civilians and other categories, then they were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's if we would have known, they would have been released, that's a theoretical answer. Because if you say if we would have known, we would have released them, at the same time there is a report that the 6.000 were not released but were exchanged as if they were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about an exchange as well, because in other theatres of war outside the corps there were such cases. And then of course, I mean, we would exchange -- well, not to say with total reciprocity, but let us say that there were exchanges in other parts of the theater of war of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would exchange civilians rather than to release them, is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not that way. It's sort of a phenomenon and good will exchange. Somebody for somebody else, whether it was one-for-one, one-for-five, whatever. I never made any decisions of that sort, and I cannot say that that was the proportion involved. If there was good will on one side, then the other side was supposed to express good will for exchanges of persons who were not military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not talking about proportions and one-to-one or one to more. I am talking about civilians being detained and where you claim that once it would have been established that they were civilians that they would be released, that the documentary evidence at least suggests that in early stages the corps command was informed about how they were captured and that the corps command was aware of civilians being exchanged and not being released. I am talking about civilians. Any comment on that? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the issue of exchanges of civilians is something that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- oh no, Mr. Traldi. I think it's time for a break. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We would like to see you back after the break. Mr. Traldi, where are we time-wise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd say roughly on track. I do expect to be the rest of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you expect to finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I expect to be the rest of today, and whether I'll require some or all of the first session tomorrow, it depends on how it develops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to seek confirmation that the videolink is functioning well. Can you hear us -- well, can you hear me, can you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear you and see the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you and we can see you as well. Mr. Traldi will now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we're returning now to this document on our screens, P230.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have the end of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we saw it was sent to the Doboj operations group, General Talic, as well as to the Main Staff. We see it's received on the 17th of July in the morning. That's a time that you were at Duge Njive at the headquarters of the Doboj operations group, as well as the forward command post of the 1 KK; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see it's sent by Colonel Vukelic, he's one of the officers who'd remained in the Banja Luka command post; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether he was in Banja Luka at the time or in Gradiska, well, he could have been because he was visiting the units, but the headquarters were in Banja Luka, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at this point, the middle of July, that's where he was, Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't say precisely whether he was there at the time, but he should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we can turn back to the first page, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is in the context of reporting on a visit by the Red Cross to the Manjaca camp, and Colonel Vukelic is reporting that the Red Cross team had broken off the discussion and visit because they hadn't been allowed to meet with four prisoners who Colonel Vukelic refers to as criminals. And he says the Red Cross team had made observations about the quantities of food, loss of weight by the prisoners and, among other things, that they had claimed to have seen fresh traces of blood on prisoners. So this is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff sent, among other things, to General Talic at OG Doboj while you were present there. In fact, at a time when General Mladic was visiting you. You were aware no later than this point, the 16th of July, that there were allegations by international organisations of abuse at Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Really it should be read to the witness what this document says, not just take something out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Traldi may put to the witness. He doesn't have to present the whole of the document to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should be able to read the document then, at least this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that part -- if there's -- let me see -- if the witness needs a bit more time then, of course, he could read the relevant lines. You perhaps, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or Mr. Traldi, if you either slowly read the portions you're interested in or if you would point at what paragraph it is so -- and then to invite the witness to read the portions you want to ask questions about. And, Mr. Lukic, there is no need for the witness to read the whole of it. If you think it's important, then in re-examination you can give him an opportunity to read the rest, and then, may I take it, demonstrate that there is more in the document which you consider to be relevant, whereas Mr. Traldi is focusing on a specific portion. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is then wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The question is entirely accurate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- based on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Traldi pointed at parts of the -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In line --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll re-read the question. No further debate at this moment. Give me just an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just ask that the witness's headphones be taken off before anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. The objection is overruled. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave a ruling, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's misrepresentation of the evidence. It says here [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the question is [B/C/S spoken]. He reported that -- I -- I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- sit down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have to sit down now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you can punish me now. Either way -- or I can misrepresent the documents as well. You have to rule that I have the right to misrepresent the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic, you know exactly how it works. First of all, I do not accept that you interrupt me and that you continue like you did. Let that be perfectly clear. That's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have to start to be impartial in this trial once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are again interrupting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do it again, measures will follow. And Mr. -- well, I saw Mr. Mladic was seeking contact. I leave it to that. Mr. Lukic, you know exactly if there's any misrepresentation, what you say is -- could I invite Mr. Traldi to read the portions --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- he wants -- again, you're interrupting me, Mr. Lukic, because I fear that it does not reflect exactly what the report says. That's the appropriate way of doing it. I have overruled your objection. Mr. Traldi has heard the discussion which I wished would not have taken place. I leave it in his hands how to proceed. And in re-examination, you have all opportunities to further explore the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have the top of page 2 in the B/C/S. I think that will include the text that Mr. Lukic is interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Your question was in connection with paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is not a way to intervene. I told you what you can do later. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The portion I'm directing your attention to now, sir, in the context of this report about the Red Cross visit to Manjaca camp, reads: "They claimed to have seen fresh traces of blood," which I put to you is on the prisoners. It then adds: "They had no answer to the question of the prisoner commander as to why they had not allowed a doctor (one of the prisoners) to establish that immediately." What I'm putting to you is as of this point, the 16th of July, 1992, when this report was sent to OG Doboj, where you and General Talic were present, General Mladic on that day, too, it's clear the 1st Krajina Corps and the Main Staff knew there were allegations by the Red Cross that prisoners were being abused at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me explain. I was at the command post in Duge Njive, some 20 kilometres from Doboj. I do not recall having had this contact or having received this report with this content. I did not leave -- it wasn't a command post per se. It was an observation post where one could observe the battle-field from. I wasn't at the command post so as to be able to read the reports of commissions. My main task was to control the unit; specifically, I cannot recall this situation involving this Red Cross team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that just days later, between 10 days and two weeks later, the guards at Manjaca reported in one of their regular reports to Colonel Bogojevic that two of the prisoners, Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender, had been killed. Do you recall that evidence being discussed among the corps command?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that they were killed, that the perpetrators were found, prosecuted, and sentenced. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, though, how it all came to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say the perpetrators were prosecuted and sentenced, that happened in 2007, approximately; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It certainly didn't happen during the war and it certainly wasn't done by the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, proceedings were initiated but I don't know when they were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, no soldiers in your corps served terms of imprisonment for crimes against Muslims and Croats, did they, during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some cases. I don't know whether judgements were handed down and proceedings completed. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you can't name one soldier in the 1st Krajina Corps that was sentenced at the conclusion of a trial to a term of imprisonment that they served during the war for crimes against Muslims or Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now and here under these conditions, I'm not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness. Mr. Kelecevic, you just said: "There were some cases." What do you mean by that? Can you give some more details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I can say something about this case because the last name Filipovic rings a bell. I know that the case was processed, the person was sentenced, and the case was closed. I learned about that from an officer of mine who at the time was -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You already told about that case. You said: "There were some cases." Can you please explain which cases do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I can't enumerate individually some 25 years later. To be honest, my memory isn't the best anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said you learned about the case of Filipovic from an officer of yours. Which officer was that and when did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard about the case. I think it was this Major or Lieutenant-Colonel Lukajic, Dane Lukajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When did he tell you about the Filipovic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to say. I can't tell you now in terms of date. I don't know when he told me about it, but I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: During the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P221, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just returning to what the corps knew, and we don't need it for -- we just need it on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Because it's under seal, I'd ask that we just keep page 1 in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from Manjaca camp to the 1st Krajina Corps' intelligence and security section dated 22 July 1992. It would have gone to Colonel Bogojevic as part of the camp's regular reporting to him; right? Sir, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this would have gone to Colonel Bogojevic as part of the camp guards' regular reporting to him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that it was sent to the intelligence and security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what we read here is it should be noted that: "Every new group of prisoners from Kljuc and Sanski Most is less and less incriminated, so we suggest that cases are selected, i.e., that this way of bringing of 'prisoners' is stopped, because if they did not have weapons, did not participate in activities and give any form of resistance, then such people cannot be treated as war prisoners, nor be brought to the POW camp. Incidentally, this camp can be considered as a detention camp, i.e., a camp for segregation of Muslims and Croats, which history will not forgive us." So the corps command knew as of the 22nd of July, 1992 and contrary to what you said earlier about not knowing what was going on in Manjaca until August, knew that the guards at the camp were reporting that this was a detention camp, a camp for segregation, and a camp full of prisoners who didn't have weapons and didn't give any form of resistance. The corps command knew all that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have known. I cannot say specifically for this document whether it was presented as such to the corps command or whether it was conveyed to them ad lib.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have just three quick questions to close the topic of Manjaca. We entered into this, in part, discussing exchanges. The people who were held at Manjaca that were exchanged, they were exchanged out of Republika Srpska into the Bosnian-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question. I did not hear the question. I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can hear you. I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you. I can hear you, too. The people who were held at Manjaca --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Wait a moment and I'll repeat it. The people who were held at Manjaca that were exchanged, they were exchanged out of Republika Srpska into Bosnian- and Croat-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't -- I don't know whether it was territory controlled by the Bosniak or Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But out of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but most probably. I don't know where they were sent to. Perhaps -- well, I don't know if it concerns the POWs handed over in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those were sent out of the country entirely into Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the Sava and into Croatia. They weren't sent out of the country because Slavonia, for the most part, is inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's the ones who were sent across the Sava. Hundreds of other detainees at that time were instead transferred to Batkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified earlier that General Talic ordered the camp to be set up. Now as a matter of principle, is that something he would have done on his own or something that he would have consulted with his superior, General Mladic, about?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he consulted Mr. Mladic, but I suppose with regards to the principle of subordination that it was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It would have been his obligation; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the prisoners that were sent out of the Republika Srpska, of course, even if there had been any desire to send any of them home, it would have been impossible because many of their homes and villages had been destroyed by VRS units in Kljuc and Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose all of that was possible because many houses had been destroyed. I suppose that these persons could no longer go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Many houses had been destroyed in Kljuc and Sanski Most in Muslim villages by VRS forces; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let's make a distinction here. Kljuc was not in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps, whereas Sanski Most was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Many houses had been destroyed in Kljuc and Sanski Most in Muslim villages by VRS forces; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't speak about Kljuc because it was outside the AOR. As for Sanski Most, there was combat and forces on both sides contributed to the destruction of the area. I cannot assert that only the Serb forces were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Destruction of homes in Muslim villages, Mahala, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Lukavica, that was done by VRS forces, the 6th Brigade under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably most of the Muslim houses were destroyed during those combat operations. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again you are evasive in your answers. The question clearly focuses on whether the destruction was done by the VRS. Now, you again and again then say it happened during combat operations. Could you please specifically in relation to the villages mentioned, Mahala, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Lukavica, could you tell us whether, to your knowledge, the destruction of houses was done by Serb forces or by any other force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be specific in answering that question because I was at least 150 kilometres to the east away from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you said that you couldn't tell us anything about Kljuc because it was not your area of responsibility. Now you're saying you can't tell us anything about these villages because you were away. Sometimes you may gain knowledge of events even if you're not personally present. Did you ever learn anything about the destruction of houses in the villages mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did learn about that through reports that there was combat in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just that there was combat, nothing about destruction of houses by VRS forces or by any other force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say who it was that carried out the destruction. There was combat and we know what things are like when there is combat. In a built-up area, there has to be destruction, destruction of buildings. I know that in that area, as far as Sanski Most is concerned, Kljuc was not in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. These are municipalities that are adjacent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're talking about destruction of buildings. Destruction of houses inhabited by families, persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about destruction during combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For one reason or another, you seem to be hesitant to answer the questions that are put to you. I invite you to be less evasive and rather focus your answers on the questions put to you. Mr. Traldi will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to close the topic of Manjaca for the moment, sir. You'd used the term "individual cases" when you were describing the abuse that the corps knew to have occurred there. The detention of more than 6.000 civilians and their eventual removal through exchange, that's a massive operation. It's a policy not an individual case; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that that's a general policy. I mean, quite simply, that was a camp that took people in. And, as far as I know, 9.000 or 6.000, whatever it was that you said, I mean, it -- I do not remember that there were ever that many persons there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It again doesn't answer the question, Witness. I really urge you to answer the questions as they are put to you and not to answer questions that were not put to you. It may have an impact on the evaluation of your evidence. Please be aware of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn now to Kljuc now. The 30th Partizan Division, that was a 5th Corps unit in the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was but later it was resubordinated to the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But in late May 1992, it was a 1st Krajina Corps unit in the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the date, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Its commander, both before and after the transformation, was Stanislav Galic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He later became commander of the SRK. That was a promotion; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He later changed positions from commander of the 30th Division to commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That was a promotion; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of your assistants, Dragan Marcetic, he was promoted to serve in the SRK with Galic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was chief of staff in the corps then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that 30th Division in late May 1992 carried out large operations in Kljuc municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that then it was not within the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has received evidence that it was reporting to the 1st Krajina Corps' duty team. It's seen communications about the 30th Partizan Division in that duty team handbook. That's the structure you'd expect if it was still -- and the communication chain you'd expect if it was still part of the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: During those operations, Muslim villages were shelled; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those operations in Kljuc, they never came up in any of the weekly meetings of the corps command dealing with subjects throughout the corps' area of responsibility which you testified that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended these meetings. But as far as Kljuc is concerned, I did not have any knowledge as to when these operations were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the end of these operations on or about the 1st of June, approximately 80 Muslim civilians detained in a school at Velagici were massacred. You're aware of that massacre; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard of that case. Again, Velagici is not within the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But the perpetrators were arrested; right? The people who murdered the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Military post 4022 in Banja Luka, what was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military post of the corps, as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what was 4022?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Post 4022, what was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a military post code. That is a code for a unit, and I cannot say now -- I mean, how could anyone expect me to know military post code numbers after all these years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's have P3528.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is going to be the Velagici case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you said P3528.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I did. I was recorded differently and I apologise for my speed. And could we have page 5 in the English and 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an Official Note from the military police at post 4627 in Banja Luka. It says it's compiled on the gathering of evidence about the killing of a large group of persons in Velagici in Kljuc on the 1st of June, that the information was received from security chief of Banja Luka military post 4022 command. That would be Colonel Bogojevic; right? Sorry, at that time Colonel Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about this investigation of the military police in Velagici. I don't know about that. Well, look, I mean, the police territorial jurisdiction does not have to be the same as that of the command of the unit. A certain unit of the military police can carry out an investigation in another territory as well, so this case, no. I know that Velagici was within the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the lead defendant in this case was named Amidzic as a military policeman. He's in the 1st Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By 1st Corps you mean the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1st Krajina Corps. 1st Krajina Corps. As for this man, Amidzic, I don't know. I don't know whether he's a military policeman. I only know of Colonel Amidzic, Colonel Bosko Amidzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have page 38 in the English and 28 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the case file. It's a letter by the detained persons to Corps Commander Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 40 in the English and 29 in the B/C/S, the end of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see that they write: "We are prepared to fight for the Serbian people in Krajina anywhere and any time, to the very end. Please, Comrade General, try to understand our situation and let us fight for the Serbian people and for Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we now turn to the next page of the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see that it's a request for an investigation, March 1993, nine months later. Nothing had happened for those nine months because the soldiers had been released back to their units after they wrote to General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I see this, but that is why I'm speaking with a lack of certainty, and I don't want it to seem that I'm hesitating again. This is Kljuc, then also Laniste, Velagici, Kljuc, all of that is outside my area of responsibility. However, the investigation organs, they work for that 2nd Krajina Corps, and I really cannot say anything about this case. I think that these soldiers are addressing Commander Talic, quite simply, so that he could take him [as interpreted] into his unit, as far as I can see, but they are not within Talic's corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You don't not have any personal knowledge as to what corps these soldiers were from. That's what you said a moment ago; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm looking at this again now. No, I don't know. I mean, how could I know individual soldiers given the thousands -- tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of soldiers that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say the number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 3817. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a report signed for Colonel Galic dated the 19th of July, 1992, from 30th Partizan Division to the command of the 19th Partizan Brigade. Turning to the bottom of page 2 in the English and B/C/S, at the bottom we read that: "At the last briefing, Generals Mladic and Talic commanded the 30th Partizan division for their results in combat operations and their high combat morale, requesting that all soldiers be informed about this commendation." I have two questions for you about this. First, General Talic is commending the unit because it's a 1st Krajina Corps unit; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Talic is commending this unit, it is probably a unit of the 1st Corps. I was not present, I mean during the commendation. During what it was that happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he and General Talic are both commending this unit -- sorry, he and General Mladic are both commending this unit that committed massive crimes against Muslims in Kljuc at the end of the month of May; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say which unit it was that did that, but I'm talking about the territory concerned, Velagici, Laniste, et cetera. That is not the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. That I do know. I can see on the basis of this now that I was in a completely different position, and I could not have been present there when they were commending someone and things like that. I simply have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P4052.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a document sent by then Colonel Galic to the 1st Krajina Corps command on the 9th of June, explanation of the resubordination of one battalion. And he explains that on the 6th of June, 1992 in the Kljuc municipal assembly building a meeting had been held with the 2nd Corps chief of staff who, on behalf of the command of the 2 KK, had informed the commander of the 30th Partizan Division, Galic, that Kljuc and the units deployed there were being resubordinated to the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Up to that point when that meeting was held, those units were under the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the date there, that is the 9th of June, and I cannot say that's the exact date when it started. I see the date here and that's when it was resubordinated then, this unit, to the 2nd Corps. And that is what I've been saying all along. And that's also what I have to say about Velagici, Laniste, Kljuc, that is the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. And that is why I, as the chief of staff, did not have any knowledge about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be totally clear, sir, and fair to you, what I'm putting to you is the operations and the crimes that we've been discussing, those occurred before this date, before this transfer of authority, were conducted by the 30th Partizan Division, which was under the 1st Krajina Corps. Those crimes were General Talic's responsibility. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because, I mean, these dates, well, I've been saying carrying out combat operations does not mean that it starts, say, from this particular day. It could have started a day or two before that. I cannot say exactly that it was under the 1st Corps. I cannot confirm that. Because I was very, very far away from that area, I mean. That zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at the time. Well, we started five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to go on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's okay if we take the break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We take a break now and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you, we can see you. Unless it's otherwise at the other side, we'll immediately now continue. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning now to Prijedor. The brigade responsible for Prijedor before the transformation was the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see on my screen that the far end microphone is switched off to start with. It's now switched on. Could we check whether you can hear us? Apparently you can't hear us. At the far end again I see on my screen that the microphone is switched off. Could you switch it on again and speak a few words.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we're having difficulty with the telephone line. The witness can hear what's being said in court, but I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that one of the connections - that is, the English one - is not functioning well, whereas the B/C/S apparently is functioning. And I again see that the far end microphone is -- and it's now switched on again. Can you now hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. We can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can continue. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, turning to Prijedor, the brigade responsible for Prijedor before the transformation was the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you are speaking very fast and the only result is that you then have to wait for a while until it is translated. If you speak slower, then it will go as fast but it will be easier for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The 343rd Brigade's commander was Vladimir Arsic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: His deputy was Radmilo Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And after the transformation, the largest VRS brigade in Prijedor was the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you will, the largest brigade, and I don't know what your criterion is for measuring it -- well, yes, in Prijedor. Yes, it's the biggest one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
