utterances.text: And the biggest one was the 43rd Brigade, Colonel Arsic was the commander, Zeljaja was his deputy; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday at transcript page 37151 that in late May 1992 the 43rd Brigade's command was still in Croatia. Did you mean to suggest that the brigade command was in Croatia during the operations in Hambarine and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now I cannot tell you exactly whether the commander or the chief -- well, one of them must have been with the brigade, and the chief most probably could have been in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31652.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an evaluation of Colonel Arsic by General Talic dated the 20th of July, 1993. Now, if we turn to page 2 in both languages, we see his scores, a lot of 5s with a couple of 4s, and the conclusion "particularly exceeds." Now, this reflects Talic's positive assessment, his endorsement of Arsic's work; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. His grades are excellent. As far as I'm concerned, I met Arsic for the first time and started working with him for the first time in 1992 upon my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you: This reflects General Talic's positive assessment and endorsement of Arsic's work; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 3 in both languages, at the top of the page we see the descriptive assessment, and in the third paragraph we see General Talic write that Arsic "led an operation on Kozarac." That's the operation in late May that you mention in your statement and that I asked you about a moment ago; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And clearly he had to be in Prijedor municipality to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 31652 receives number P7474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7474 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now focusing in on the late May period, you mention the incident at the Hambarine check-point in your statement, and you describe it as "a typical example of armed Muslims attempting to seize power." This incident occurred on or about the 22nd of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date of that. But, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, in fact, armed Serbs had seized power in Prijedor several weeks earlier; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What did Serbs do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They took over power in Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992, as you well know; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are talking about armed Serbs, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. Armed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Prijedor the Serbs had had power, even before that. I don't know. Why would they be trying to seize it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, they seized it on the 30th of April, took over the municipality building. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't mean that they took over the entire town and environs of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, several of those environs, those were only taken over once the VRS was formed through VRS operations; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which villages or areas you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, first Hambarine. You state that after the check-point incident, the army carried out an action to disarm the armed Muslim population. Now, the attack on Hambarine, that was led by the 43rd Brigade of the VRS just like the Kozarac attack; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the 43rd Brigade had communications with the corps command about negotiations with the residents of Hambarine about the ultimatum that was given them before the attack; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from reports because I wasn't there at the time. I told you where I was. You know I was at the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you know from reports, just like the corps command knew from reports, what was happening there; right? That's the basis for the information you provide in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3946, page 139 in the English and 162 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is part of the 5th Corps' war diary for the western Slavonian front, and we're looking at the 23rd of May. And directing your attention to 1715 hours, we see a report from Major Zeljaja. He mentions negotiations, a dead-line for the killers of the two soldiers on the 22nd of May to be handed over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can the B/C/S portion be enlarged with respect to item 372.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we don't need the right side of the -- no, we don't need all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So looking at the second asterisk, we see a note that the cleansing, and it uses the word "ciscenje" "of Hambarine has begun." So, first, this is a reflection of the communications between the corps command and the 43rd Brigade during that operation; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that. But I wasn't in a position to read the war diary or to be present at the command post. All of this was happening in Croatia in Slavonia, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this information is coming from Major Zeljaja because he was in Prijedor too; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was in Prijedor at that time or in Slavonia. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So when you said yesterday the command wasn't in Prijedor, it was in Croatia, your actual evidence now is that the brigade commander was in Prijedor and you don't know where his chief of staff was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You asked me if he was in Prijedor, the commander. I don't know whether Arsic was in Prijedor on that day or if he was in Slavonia. I can't confirm that. I know that the commander is always the commander, wherever he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's look at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we have to scroll down a little bit in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The first entry on the 24th of May, the 5th Partizan Brigade, that's another brigade in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it says it sent soldiers and a Pinzgauer and two armoured combat vehicles to Major Zeljaja in Prijedor. He, like Arsic, was in Prijedor commanding the Hambarine and Kozarac operations; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't confirm or deny that. I was not in the area. I can't confirm anything on the basis of this report. All I can see is that in all likelihood they were both in Prijedor, and perhaps the operations officer or a deputy remained in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know, as you sit there today, that Hambarine during what's referred to here as the cleansing of Hambarine was massively shelled and you know that Muslim civilians were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning then to Kozarac, the 43rd Brigade again had communication with the corps command about preparations for that attack; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with the commander exclusively because I was in a different sector. They had no contact with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a summary of a conversation intercepted by the Croatian authorities on the 25th of May, 1992. It starts by referring to Prijedor. It says: "Negotiations are still ongoing with the Crisis Staff of the Kozarac village." It describes what Major Zeljaja is saying about the negotiations. And then it says that: "At 0910 hours, General Talic reported to General Milovanovic that the place Kozarac was completely surrounded and blocked and the place should fall by noon tomorrow." Now, this is a reflection that the corps command also had communications with the VRS Main Staff about preparations for the attack on Kozarac during the lead-up to that attack; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. The commander talked to the Main Staff. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It would have been his responsibility to talk to the Main Staff, say, Okay, there are preparations ongoing to attack this village; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the contents of their discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Speaking in principle, I understand your evidence is that you didn't participate in those conversations yourself. Speaking in principle, General Talic wasn't running around attacking villages on his own; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He definitely wasn't running around. I suppose he was either in Banja Luka or in Prijedor. I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he also wasn't attacking on his own before the corps undertook an activity like that. As a matter of doctrine and principle, he would consult with the Main Staff; right? Just like we saw in the Corridor documents yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me, perhaps in such extraordinary circumstances he needn't need to ask for approval. He was a very experienced commander, capable of self-initiative in making decisions on his own. He may have been engaged in consultation process. In any case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was an experienced commander. General Mladic trusted him a lot; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But as an experienced commander who General Mladic trusted, he would have obeyed the chain of command and kept the Main Staff in the loop on preparations for this operation, like we saw here; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have. I can't say whether he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We always object to these type of documents, since those words were not recorded. It's Croatian intercept, I guess. So I don't know why would we accept this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Lukic's objection. For the record, my understanding is the issue is controlled by the Chamber's decision on P7198, a similar Croatian intercept that Mr. Lukic and I dealt with. The Chamber issued a decision admitting it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The document will be admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number would?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, large numbers of Muslims were killed during the Kozarac operation; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that people were killed, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Civilian property in the village was massively destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mosques were --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of houses and other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mosques were destroyed; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the prisoners taken during these operations -- well, first, the 1st Krajina Corps, its subordinate unit, the 43rd Brigade, took large numbers of prisoners during the Hambarine and Kozarac operations; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And those were taken to the Prijedor camps that you mention in your statement, Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mention in paragraph 15 of your statement a Muslim counterattack on the town of Prijedor in late April 1992. That was, in fact, on the 30th of May; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind the attack on the municipal assembly building, it was on the 30th of May as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the 43rd Brigade again had communication with the 1st Krajina Corps command during that operation as well as the ones in Hambarine and Kozarac; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And a Muslim neighbourhood called Stari Grad was destroyed by the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know what part of town that is, but, yes, in all likelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence, P2243, that that day Zeljaja called General Talic, told him that he was cleansing everything, and he wouldn't spare women and children anymore. That's a reflection, first, that Zeljaja was also in Prijedor overseeing the operations on the 30th; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I can't confirm if they were there. Perhaps both of them were, but I don't know that. As the operation was underway, the commander was informed about it. And as I said, I was on a completely different axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, cleansing everything, not sparing women and children, surely Major Zeljaja was removed from his position or replaced after telling General Talic that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him being replaced. Until the end of the war, he remained chief. Actually, later on he became the commander of that brigade. I'm not aware of his removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was promoted to colonel too; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was promoted to the rank of colonel later on, although I don't recall the date. It was sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning back to the prisoners, you know that, in fact, as you sit there today, a large proportion of the male population of Kozarac and Hambarine were rounded up and taken to the Prijedor camps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, for the most part, the Prijedor Crisis Staff did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a problem with the previously mentioned P number, 2243. Not shown to the witness, claiming from that something, and I cannot find it in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is in e-court, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried to open it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I looked at it and I can tell you that what Mr. Traldi quoted is indeed said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but obviously our system is not working then. I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know. Perhaps -- let me just check. I can tell you that, and I'll look at the source, the original, because I looked at the English translation, as you will understand. It -- at least on my computer it opens perfectly well. If you have any problems with your computer and having access to e-court, then of course -- and are you sure that you typed in the right date and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am. It is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is P0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have it in my hands now. So it's again intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: completely confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what -- one second, please. 54. Yes, we received evidence. I think that's correct. And that is admitted evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever your objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My objection is that it's not words of Zeljaja, that somebody else is claiming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may revisit that in re-examination. It doesn't say anywhere that these are -- the Chamber received evidence that, and that is exactly what is found in that evidence. Whether you consider the source such that it should be dealt with in a different way, you can explore that. This is what the evidence says, among others. You may deal with it later. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed. And if you have any problems in your e-court access, then of course we'll seek to have you assisted to get it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, it's not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not working. Then we'll seek assistance for you. Mr. Traldi, meanwhile, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I do, I'd just request a redaction at lines 15 and 16 of page 56, and I'm happy to explain the reasons in private session or out of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, will you please prepare the redaction. And I think for everyone who has followed the proceedings know more or less what the reason is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said, for the most part, the Prijedor Crisis Staff did that when I asked about the rounding up of the male population --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Overlapping speakers] ... proceedings, we've lost sound again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently we have a sound problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give a few words to see whether the sound is now received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we seem to have a technical problem. We cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you now hear us? The microphone at the other side is off from what we see on our screens. Is the audio still not functioning at the far end of the videolink? Witness, can you hear us in your language? I think I saw the witness saying something but since the microphone was switched off --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it's only the English channel, despite having established the connection again, what we saw a minute ago, it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We have a technical problem. I mean, I've been trying to say that. We can't hear anything that's happening in the English. Okay. Can you let the court officer know because they seem to be continuing. Yeah, but they seem to continue because I can't hear what they're saying, the Court. Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break now of 20 minutes. Madam Registrar is requested to inform the far end of the videolink by telephone that we take a break of 20 minutes and that we would like to see, but perhaps even more important hear them back at 20 minutes from now. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we try to continue, I'd like to verify whether the videolink is functioning well, both video and audio.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. We can hear and see you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear and see you as well. Mr. Traldi may therefore proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Now, during the operations at the end of May, the VRS had rounded up thousands of people who were taken to those three camps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention in your statement that Omarska and Keraterm were under the civilian police. The commander of Trnopolje was Slobodan Kuruzovic. He was under the command of the 43rd Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know Kuruzovic personally. I know that the Crisis Staff was in charge of these, well, camps, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Kuruzovic was a member of the Crisis Staff. He was also under the command of the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he was recorded as such, but I don't know whether he was in the unit. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in Omarska -- let me start the question differently. Do you know who Colonel Majstorovic was?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally. He was a colonel who had come from Varazdin. He was born there near Prijedor -- Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I ask about him in the context of Omarska because he was one of the people who supervised the teams interrogating prisoners there; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know what his purview was as far as prisoners were concerned, because I did not come across him. Although I know him personally well because he was an officer under my command before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, a Defence witness named Miso Rodic testified that Majstorovic was sent to Omarska by the 1st Krajina Corps command. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, that the command sent anyone to TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we're not talking about a TO staff. We're talking about Omarska camp. That's where Majstorovic was; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry. Sorry. Yes, yes. Not TO staffs. Crisis Staffs. The corps command did not send anyone to Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Again, we're not talking about a Crisis Staff. We're talking about Omarska camp. That's where Colonel Majstorovic was sent. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was there, but I don't know whether he was at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who sent him to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor, most probably -- well, I'm not sure about that. Let's be clear on that. I'm not a personnel officer, so I have no way of nothing. But most probably since he was born in the area, maybe he was sent there. Because he was very ill at the time and he died soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered a number of possible questions, I'm sure, but not the one I asked. Who sent Majstorovic to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who sent him. It certainly wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence from an RS MUP official named Predrag Radulovic, who was in Omarska at the time, that already in June 1992 prisoners were being abused and some were killed. And it would have been Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic's responsibility to inform the corps command of that too; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Witness. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a name here of a dead man, so I think it would be fair at least to tell us what Prosecution thinks that the Chamber receives as an evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman never testified in front of this Chamber. I don't know if he's a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He's a 92 quater witness. So it's that evidence I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the number, so I can follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll pull it up while the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Mr. Traldi will provide Mr. Lukic with the information he is requesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has received evidence that RS MUP officials present in Omarska at the time knew that prisoners were being abused there, some were killed. It would have been Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic's obligation to inform the corps command of that too; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge about his reporting. If he was reporting to Bogojevic, who was his security organ, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So your evidence is: Did you or did you not know that prisoners were being abused and killed in Omarska in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So one of your subordinate units takes 7.000 prisoners to the camps in Prijedor. Did the 1st Krajina Corps command do anything to check on the conditions?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the corps command did something with regard to that matter. I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, again, your view, as an excellent chief of staff, is you have no idea what conditions 7.000 prisoners taken by your corps were being held in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- well, this is what I know: The units of the 343rd Brigade, they did that, what you refer to just now, handed it over to the civilian authorities, and then they were responsible for everything else that was done in relation to these people. The 1st Corps practically had, I mean, well, it's not that they did anything with regard to these prisons that were under the authority of the civilian organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If these prisoners had been of any security interest, then you would have kept an eye on them. You would have wanted to know what they said during interrogations, you would have wanted to ensure that the camps were guarded so they couldn't get out; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was no longer the security organ. And I did not work in operative terms so that I could know, I mean, what was going on in a security sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The entire corps command, including the chief of staff, if there were 7.000 prisoners of legitimate security interest, it would have been an enormous issue for the corps to know how thoroughly they were being secured and to know what information they were revealing when they were interrogated; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They should know, but I physically - physically or mentally - I could not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the same question as previous one, long question, so it's not verbatim but it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have any real idea what Mr. Lukic is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is it? There is nothing verbatim, but the question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same. Whether there was any interest in those prisoners by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The -- and I have the right to insist on an answer to the question that the witness had evaded the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, is your objection: Question asked, question answered? Is that the gist of your objection? If that's the case, Mr. Traldi has responded to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I think that the witness answered on the page 63, lines 23 to 25, about his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he can assist any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Traldi wants to test, I think, that evidence, and to a certain extent that's allowed in cross-examination. Please proceed. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask the question again just for the clarity of the record. The entire corps command, including the chief of staff, if there were 7.000 prisoners of legitimate security interest, it would have been an enormous issue for the corps to know how thoroughly they were being secured and to know what information they were revealing when they were interrogated; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, interested. I'm not saying I wasn't interested, but through my logistics assistants and others for security, in a way I did learn that they were there and that this was under the control of the civilian authorities. Now, that is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, sir, you haven't again answered my question. Let me put it to you very simply: The only way that you could sit there today and suggest that you didn't know and you weren't interested in what they were being questioned about is if, just like in the Manjaca documents we saw before, these prisoners were picked up non-selectively, were not of any security interest, and so the VRS, after rounding them up, could just hand them over to the police that were securing Omarska and Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I had information that my commander, General Talic, was informed in detail by his subordinate organs, and he was there. And why should I be checking on my commander? I never did any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So your evidence now is General Talic knew in detail about the conditions at Omarska and the people being held there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say in detail, but I believe that through the chain of command he was informed about these things. I was much further away and I was attending to other tasks, specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When I put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are recorded as having said that General Talic was informed in detail. Now, if that is a mistake, of course, we could verify whether the interpretation and the transcription is correct or not. If you, however, say I may have said that, then -- and, Mr. Lukic, you may have followed the evidence in the original language, then of course there is no need to do that. But if you think that you are misinterpreted and you are misrecorded, then we'll check it and then we'll find out whether you said that General Talic was -- knew in detail about the conditions. What is it you'd like us to do, to verify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not that word "in detail," because I could never say "detaljno," I don't know whether it's been interpreted in a different way, but I'll telling you now that he was informed because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we are just checking the accuracy of the interpretation and the transcription. It will be checked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, one of the ways he was informed, as I had started off putting to you, was through Colonel Majstorovic who was deployed to Omarska to assist in overseeing the teams of investigators or interrogators; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what was supposed to be done. Now, I don't know whether he did actually do that. Majstorovic was supposed to inform his first superior officer and that was Bogojevic, if that's the way it was. Stevo Bogojevic then reports to his commander, Talic, because he is his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just to ensure that my questions have been clear, sir, a moment ago, I talked about handing over the people taken to Omarska and Keraterm to the police that were securing those facilities. You're aware that VRS units assisted in securing the facilities, even though the commanders were from the police; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want this evidence where it was proven that in Omarska and Keraterm military officers were guarding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There is substantial evidence. Among it, we can find P2900, which is the report up to the CSB on the camps in August 1992. For Keraterm, Zigic's unit's participation is reflected. Mr. Lukic and I are both familiar with that from Witness Rodic's examination. From Omarska, I think the external ring of security being done by the VRS is not even disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The external ring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: External ring outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Traldi may suggest whatever he wants in his question. It's not that in cross-examination the examiner is limited to what specific evidence he was specify. This is what Mr. Traldi puts to the witness, this is leading, that's what is allowed in cross-examination. So, therefore, your objection is apart from that Mr. Traldi, as he explained to us, apparently has a good basis for suggesting this to the witness, but he doesn't need that. Let that be clear before you raise another objection. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were those rules in force when we were cross-examining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will show you that they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please make a written submission. And we've earlier seen that the claim for, and I checked it always very carefully, the claim that we changed the rules depending on what stage of the case presentation we are is not accurate. But make whatever submissions you would like to make in this respect, Mr. Lukic. Of course, if that's what you want to refer to, of course you should not, at the detriment of a witness, make a totally unfair suggestion. There are limits also in there. That's the only thing I add at this moment to what I said before. And Mr. Traldi may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to re-ask the question very quickly: Are you aware, yes or no, that VRS soldiers assisted in securing Omarska and Trnopolje [sic], although the camps were commanded by members of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that members of the VRS provided any kind of security for securing the camps. Those two camps. We can discuss Manjaca, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to the events of late July 1992 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32733.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a daily combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff dated the 19th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have point 4 on page 2 in the English and 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see that Colonel Vukelic, who's drafted the report or who has signed the report, is reporting that the Banja Luka area is relatively stable and Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc are "fully under our control." It's correct that Prijedor municipality was fully under the VRS's control as of the 19th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we are talking about the town itself. But as for the camp facility itself and whether it was under full control, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the municipality, though. So let's set the camps aside for a moment. The territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7476 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, could I ask perhaps a few questions to the witness, especially in relation to Omarska. Witness, in your statement, you say that you know that disarmed members of the Muslim forces were taken mostly to Keraterm and Omarska. Were those prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not prisoners of war. They were, as we called them, prisoners or those who were captured but not prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to me that when armed forces capture members of the opposing forces and disarm them and deprive them of their liberty how they could be anything else than prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the participation of VRS units consisted only of bringing in those people and handing them over at the camp. Any further interrogations were conducted by civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said we disarmed them and they were members of the armed forces, but what was then the title under which they were detained if they were not prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I can't say that they were soldiers. Some may not have been. But they held on to their weapons and they did not hand them over when there was a request made to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I read your statement. "What I do know is that disarmed members of the Muslim forces ..." Are you now telling us that members of the armed forces which were carrying weapons were not soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It needn't be someone sporting a weapon. They hid weapons in their homes and elsewhere. So a weapon in and of itself does not indicate that someone is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but your statement doesn't say "persons having hidden weapons were disarmed." You say members of the Muslim armed force. So a member of an opposing armed force carrying a weapon, is that not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I said that they were members of armed forces, then I misspoke. They were members who were armed and had weapons or were suspected of having weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said that you disarmed members of the Muslim forces. That's what is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by the fact that the people who were disarmed were the ones who had weapons but did not have an authorisation to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they civilians then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if one is a civilian carrying a weapon, they still must have a licence or approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question is whether they were civilians. If you explain to us why they were carrying weapons but were apparently not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case -- sorry. I can't tell you if they were soldiers or not. We would need to check registers or documents to see whether they were members of an armed formation or not. I can't say whether specific cases, specific people were civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you've given that same explanation for Manjaca camp. You said, Well, it needed to be investigated whether they were members of the opposing armed forces. Apparently you captured them. Did you think that capturing them brings any responsibility for finding out whether or not they are or they are not soldiers, combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion in any case is that it needs to be established whether they were fighters or not. In the specific case of Omarska, I think it should have been established, and that should have been done by civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they were fighters, if you arrested them, if you disarmed them, why do you consider them not to be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were fighters and were disarmed, then of course they were POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you handed them over to the civilian authorities if you would have arrested what you say may have been prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They should have been handed over, and the ministries of defence needed to establish through records whether they belonged to the armed forces or to a unit belonging to the Muslim Croat formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say you can't tell us if the prisoners were soldiers or not. You also don't know whether they were civilians who didn't give up arms. You don't know who because they were picked up non-selectively, civilians detained along with members of what Muslim formations existed in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't be established straight away, as I said, whether the person in question was a civilian or someone who had been assigned to a unit. I can't tell you now whether anyone in particular was a civilian or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to move away from the camps now. Before I do, just a quick correction to the transcript. At temporary transcript page 69, lines 2 and 3, I'm recorded to have referred to Omarska and Trnopolje. I certainly intended to refer to Omarska and Keraterm, and I think that was how Mr. Lukic understood me, I hope, when I was referring to camps where soldiers assisted but the police were in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any concern that the witness may have been confused by it? If so, then please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to ask him, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you verify, Mr. Traldi, if there is any --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when I was asking you about camps where the commanders were members of the civilian police but I suggested to you the military assisted in securing -- or members of the military assisted in securing, did you understand me to be referring to Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mentioned Trnopolje, I think you were confused because I don't know how to describe Trnopolje but I think it was more of an open-type facility with less stringent controls, and basically the people were being taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'd asked you a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask for a direct answer. When I asked you about camps where the commanders were members of the civilian police but the military or members of the military assisted in securing the facilities, you understood me to be talking about Omarska and Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes. Because I know Trnopolje only as the facility that I've just tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I have last -- one final question for you in relation to the matters we have discussed over the last hour, approximately. If there is doubt as to whether a person is a civilian or a combatant, how should you treat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I need to treat them humanely. It needs to be established through an interview without any mistreatment or applying physical force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could he be deprived of his liberty just to find out whether he is a civilian or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, depriving of liberty is not necessary. The person may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he has no choice than to be brought in, that's what we call depriving of liberty or detention. Could you please answer my question. I didn't ask whether it's necessary or not, but my question was whether you can deprive someone of his liberty just to find out whether he's a civilian or not. And you may include bringing him in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should not deprive him of his liberty. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He shouldn't be deprived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He should also not be brought in against his will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be in favour of establishing the identity. Now, whether we call it bringing in or not is a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let me be very clear. Bringing in someone against his will and then to keeping him for, well, let's say more than one, two, or three days against his will, I consider that to be deprivation of liberty. Is that -- if you don't know whether he is civilian or not, would that be admissible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not acceptable to keep someone that long for that reason. It is not an optimum solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that people, you said you would have to find out whether they were civilians or not, that they were kept for far longer than two or three days in camps? And I'm specifically referring to Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that decision should have been made by those engaged in that work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, before we turned back to the camps, we'd confirmed that as of the 19th of July, Prijedor municipality was fully under VRS control. You're aware that there were large cleansing operations by the VRS in the Brdo and Ljubija areas of Prijedor over the next approximately a week; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm. I have to repeat that again. I cannot confirm that because I did not receive regular reports from the command because of the task I had been assigned previously. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the 1st Krajina Corps command was well aware of the massacre at Brisevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember at all the area of Brisevo. I don't even know where it is now that you ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32810.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as it comes up, the Chamber has received evidence that the attack on Brisevo occurred during the week that I described, roughly the 20th to the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, your last answer says you don't remember the area of Brisevo. You don't even know where it is. Did you ever hear about the massacre at Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to tell you the truth, even if I had heard about it, I may have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So this is a letter from Bishop Komarica to General Talic dated the 22nd of August, 1992, entitled: "Prevent further crimes against defenceless Catholics in Ljubija area, Prijedor municipality." Turning to page 2 in the English and the B/C/S, we see at the top of the page in the B/C/S a reference to the panic that people were in because of the terrible massacre of innocent residents of the nearby village of Brisevo where dozens of men, women, and children were killed. The 1st Krajina Corps command was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where should we look in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's about halfway down the first paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is one of the ways that the 1st Krajina Corps command was informed of the massacre that had happened in Brisevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. What we see here, this letter from Bishop Komarica to General Talic is one of the ways in which the 1st Krajina Corps command was informed of the massacre in Brisevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm anything with regard to this specific case, because I don't remember Talic informing me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has evidence, P3820, that the corps command knew that people were murdered, crimes were committed by VRS soldiers in Carakovo during the same week. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence, P161, that the 1st Krajina Corps command informed the Main Staff of the murder of prisoners in room 3 at Keraterm again that same week. Is it your evidence that you also weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about those murders at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And a Defence witness named Vojo Kupresanin testified that he went to Brisevo after the massacre with officers from the 1st Krajina Corps who audio-recorded the surviving residents talking about the massacre that had happened there. Is it your evidence that you somehow missed the information then too?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I missed it. I objectively could not have known about it. That's what I've been trying to tell you. As far as for what Kupresanin did, I cannot accept your assertion because I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just so that I'm completely clear with you, what I'm putting to you is at regular meetings you received reports on what was happening throughout the corps' area of responsibility, you confirmed that, and your evidence that somehow the corps command was aware of these massive crimes against Muslims and Croats in Prijedor but you managed to avoid any knowledge, your evidence is not the truth. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do not accept that I'm not telling the truth. If I don't remember something or if I wasn't informed of things, then I can't say "yes" or "no." I allow for the possibility that since I was at the command post I did not attend each and every meeting, and that's why it can happen that I wasn't present. I know about Keraterm. As for the rest, I either don't know or don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You know about the massacre at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the massacre at Keraterm. There were two killings, but I don't know under what circumstances. As I said, the military police did not interrogate anyone inside the camp nor did any other military body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you've shown to the witness the letter by the bishop, which is still a 65 ter number. At the same time, it looks as if it's taken from a collection and not the original letter. I don't know whether you want to tender it. But if you wish to do that, then the Chamber would like you to explain to us why you consider this, published in a book apparently at page 370 or 372, why you consider this to be corresponding with a real letter that has been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's Bishop Komarica's book that it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, you hadn't explained that to us, as a matter of fact. And he then says that this is the letter he sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, and I'll find the page references for how he describes that and speak with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that we -- another matter is, do you tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, though now given the Chamber's questions, I'm willing to postpone that if it suits. But I would intend to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or have it marked for identification for the time being pending your discussions with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32810 receives number P7477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7477 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this document we see in front of us reassigns Colonel Arsic to be commander of the Doboj operations group. It's dated the 27th of May, 1993. As an operations group involves several brigades, this is a promotion for him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 31653 receives number P7478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7478 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P358, page 151 in the English and 155 in the B/C/S original, not transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we see here the beginning of a meeting on the 27th of May, 1993, in one of General Mladic's notebooks from the war, 27th of May, the same document we saw for the date of General Arsic's - then Colonel Arsic's promotion, a moment ago. Turning to page 154 at the bottom in English and 158 in the original B/C/S, we see Colonel Bogojevic speaking. That's a reference to the 1st Krajina Corps' assistant commander for security at the time; right? Sir, I asked you a very simple question. That Colonel Bogojevic we see referred to there, that's the 1 KK assistant commander for security; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At that time, May 1993, you would have been in very regular contact with him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Meeting daily?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't have to mean that. Why would we have to be in contact every day?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How regularly were you in contact with him at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said when necessary. Usually once a week. The security organ is personally responsible to the commander. Not the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did Colonel Bogojevic attend General Talic's morning meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard evidence from Bosko Amidzic, a Defence witness, who is the assistant commander for logistics at this time, that there was a morning meeting daily. You attended those meetings with Colonel Bogojevic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings were not held every morning. Usually it was Monday when the command would meet, if necessary. There weren't meetings held every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll leave that point aside for the moment. What we see General Mladic record here is that Simo Drljaca -- or Colonel Bogojevic is informing him that Simo Drljaca arrived, that he'd been sent by the minister of the RS MUP about the Tomasica mine. Turning to the next page in both languages, General Mladic records this is near Prijedor where earlier they'd buried around 5.000 Muslims, and Colonel Bogojevic records -- or sorry, General Mladic records under Colonel Bogojevic's name that they want to get rid of it by burning, grinding, or some other way. Now, first, you knew, just like General Mladic and Colonel Bogojevic, that large numbers of Muslims had been killed in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that a larger number of people were killed in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you repeat where you heard that a larger number of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it was Kozarac and Omarska. But as for numbers, I mean, I cannot deal with that now. Tomasica, as we see here, now, I was not aware of any of that at all. I wasn't aware of Tomasica at all as a place where that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So we see here there are all kinds of bodies, they have involved Subotic in this. "The team includes Drljaca. He was in charge even while this was being done at the meeting where General Subotic, Arsic, Drljaca, me, and Mile Matijevic." So Colonel Bogojevic, he's had meetings about this in Prijedor, he's informing General Mladic, it's your position he never told you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a position. But it is possible that something like that was done too because he's the security organ and he thought -- well, I don't know, maybe he didn't trust us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He would have told Talic though; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot assert that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm putting to you is it's impossible that the corps command was ignorant of this and that it reflects that you're understating today the massive human consequences of the VRS's campaign in Prijedor, that a huge number of Muslims were killed in Prijedor municipality, not just in Kozarac and Omarska but in the many, many massacres that the corps command knew about and you claimed a moment ago you'd avoided knowledge of. That's the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not put it that way. First of all, because I am saying what it is that I know. I don't want people to put words into my mouth or into my head. I know what I spoke about. What I don't know about, I am not going to speak of. So I would totally disagree. I do not agree that I was not telling the truth. Throughout my life, I've just been telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I just say one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it is in direct answer to the question, you may. Otherwise, you should refrain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's time to adjourn for the day. Witness, I give you the same instructions as I did yesterday - that is, that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given yesterday and today or still to be given tomorrow. Perhaps we already disconnect the videolink. I would have a very short question to the parties. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see the videolink is disconnected. Mr. Traldi, as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll certainly stay within my estimate, and I haven't checked exactly what that is or what that leaves me, but I will -- I'll be within my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is some concern that some of the evidence you are eliciting from this witness is repetitious. It overlaps with evidence we've seen before. You apparently are aware of it because you often have referred the witness to it. And the second issue is to what extent it's necessary to push the witness if he says he doesn't have knowledge about certain things, also in view how the cross-examination developed until now. Would you please keep that in mind when further preparing. Mr. Lukic, any indication as to how much time you would need, as matters stand now, having heard the bulk of the cross-examination, how much time you'd need for the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll have a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I know that -- I am sure that we will not finish tomorrow with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, of course, the question arises whether we will finish with the next witness on Thursday. I mean, what happens, Mr. Lukic, is that you present a witness which gives rather blank statements about events with a very broad picture, and that of course triggers the Prosecution to find out what the witness really knows about all that. And I think already at the beginning of this testimony, I said something about sources of knowledge being all pretty unclear in the statement. So part of what happens, I would say, is also triggered by the way in which you take and present statements. Therefore, I would urge you to see whether we can conclude the evidence of this witness and the next witness by this Thursday, and I would further like to add that the Chamber needs some time to deal with a few procedural matters. I think we could deal with them in approximately half an hour, perhaps up to 40 minutes, and the parties are invited to seek an agreement on how to use the hours in the remaining two days. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 15th of July, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
